title: Exxon Stock Rises as Oil Nears $92 on Hormuz Risk - TradingView
content: Exxon Mobil XOM, the integrated oil-and-gas powerhouse, rose approximately 0.5% to $166.47 Wednesday as Brent crude marched toward $92 per barrel. Oil hit roughly a three-week high as constrained shipping through the Strait of Hormuz kept supply fears alive and the Middle East risk premium elevated. For Exxon, the math is simple: expensive oil means more cash flowing through an already enormous upstream machine. The supply story is getting tighter from multiple directions. Reuters reported that Russian oil exports from western ports ran roughly 15% below plan during the first half of August. Exxon hardly needs much help from oil prices to generate serious cash. The company delivered second-quarter earnings of $14.5 billion, free cash flow of $17.2 billion and operating cash flow of $23.6 billion. Now throw stronger crude pricing into that machine, and the earnings setup gets even more interesting. But investors are already paying for plenty of good news. At $166.47, Exxon trades 32.85% above its GF Value estimate of $125.31. That is a serious premium, and it raises the bar. Record Permian production, refining scale and monster cash generation give Exxon fundamental firepower beyond any geopolitical spike, but $92 oil remains a powerful tailwind. If Hormuz shipping normalizes or diplomacy cools the Middle East risk premium, crude could retreat fast. For now, Exxon has both operational momentum and oil prices working in its favorthe question is how much of that strength is already sitting inside a $166.47 stock price. title: ExxonMobil’s Return Comes From Somewhere The Index Does Not Go - Trefis
content: A five-year correlation this low is not a statistical curiosity; it is what an earnings stream built on barrels and product margins looks like beside the index. ExxonMobil (XOM) has gained 4.3% over the last five trading days while the S&P 500 slipped 0.5%, and a stock rising while the tape sags is the kind that gets chased. But the question that decides your outcome is different: how much of this return is its own story rather than the index you already own, and what owning it does to your swings. On five years of evidence, most of that return is not the index. Most Of What Moves This Stock Is Not What Moves The Index Over the past five years ExxonMobil’s correlation to the S&P 500 has been 0.26, on a scale where 1.0 would mean lockstep. Gold, the asset investors hold precisely because it does its own thing, correlates to this stock at 0.1 over the same five years. The index reading is higher, and still describes a stock that has largely moved independently of the broad market. That independence has not cost return, though it has cost calm: the stock annualized 30.2% over that window against 13.2% for the index, at 26.7% volatility versus 17.2%. Barrels And Product Margins Are What Set This Return Stream That independence comes from what the company sells. In the second quarter of 2026 ExxonMobil lost roughly 10% of its upstream production to the Middle East conflict and still earned $14.5 billion. By its own account, its North American facilities met the supply shortfall that disruption created, driving a roughly 180% increase in chemical product margins versus the first quarter of 2026, while its Gulf Coast refining operations answered a tight diesel market with record second quarter diesel production. That is the operating reality behind a low correlation: earnings that answer to oil supply and product margins. The quarter threw off $23.6 billion of cash flow from operations. Cash generation of that kind is one of the properties the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for. Over The Past Year It Tended To Rise On The Market’s Down Days The capture readings, which measure the share of the index’s move the stock caught over a one-year window rather than five, show something stronger than independence. On days the S&P 500 fell over the past year, ExxonMobil moved about 110% in the opposite direction, tending to rise as the index dropped. On the market’s up days it moved about 32% of the index’s move in the opposite direction, tending to fall when the index rose. That is counter-cyclical rather than muted, and both halves are one trait: the cushion on a bad week is paid for by giving some back on the good ones. A one-year reading can shift. What Would Undo The Margin Support Is Capacity Coming Back The role it can play, then, is a return engine the index does not supply, bought at a wider swing. What would change it is what created it: management counts roughly 3 million barrels a day of capacity missing from the market, and expects a robust refining market with very high margins while that holds. Watch for that supply returning, because the margin support behind these earnings goes when it does. The swing is the price of the independence. A stock that moves on its own is still one company’s exposure to one commodity cycle, and that cushion is a byproduct, not a substitute for spreading risk. The Trefis High Quality Portfolio is built the other way around, spreading that risk across quality businesses. title: Targa Resources' Stock Near 52-Week High: Time to Lock in Gains? - theglobeandmail.com
content: Shares of Targa Resources Corp.TRGP closed at $297.77 on Tuesday, near its 52-week high of $305.08, following a surge of 85.2% in a year. The stock price rally was followed by a positive long-term agreement with ExxonMobil Holdings CorporationXOM across the Permian.During the same time period, the company’s shares outperformed the sub-industry and the broader oil and energy sector’s rise of 51.6% and 37.6%, respectively. Peer comparison further highlights the strength, as Targa Resources conveniently outpaced its peers: Sunoco LPSUN and Western Midstream Partners, LPWES, which climbed 48.8% and 30.4%, respectively, in the past year. Targa Resources continues to benefit from strong demand for its Permian and Gulf Coast midstream network, enabling the company to convert this demand into steady and durable cash flows. Headquartered in Houston, TX, Targa Resources operates at the center of the U.S. midstream energy infrastructure and delivers essential services across the natural gas and natural gas liquids (NGL) value chain. Its operations include gathering, treating, compressing, processing, transporting and storing these resources. The company runs its business through two main segments — Gathering & Processing and Logistics & Transportation. A significant portion of Targa Resources’ revenues comes from fee-based contracts, which help provide a relatively stable income stream even during periods of commodity price volatility. That said, investors are now weighing whether TRGP’s strong rally still has room to continue or if much of its future growth is already priced into the stock. With solid momentum and an encouraging outlook, the company’s prospects merit a closer look before deciding whether to buy, hold or lock in profits. Long-Term Growth Visibility From ExxonMobil Agreements: Targa Resources’ new 20-year agreements with ExxonMobil provide strong long-term volume visibility and reinforce its growth outlook. The contracts add significant acreage dedications across the Permian Delaware and Midland basins, covering gathering, processing, treating, NGL transportation and fractionation through 2046. The agreements are expected to drive substantial volume growth across TRGP’s integrated infrastructure and support growth well into the next decade. New processing plants and the Bull Run II pipeline further position the company to capture rising Permian production, supporting durable and growing adjusted free cash flow. A Positive 2026 Earnings Estimate: The Zacks Consensus Estimate for TRGP’s 2026 earnings is pegged at $11.01 per share, indicating 29.7% year-over-year growth. Additionally, the consensus mark for 2026 revenues is pegged at $19.12 billion, also implying a 12.3% year-over-year rise. The positive earnings estimate outlook makes the stock attractive for investors. In comparison to Targa Resources, the Zacks Consensus Estimate of the above-mentioned peer companies, namely Sunoco and Western Midstream, also indicates positive year-over-year growth for 2026. Strong Permian Volume Growth Supports Long-Term Earnings: Targa Resources is benefiting from robust producer activity across the Permian Basin, with second-quarter volumes reaching a record 7.2 Bcf/d, up 7% sequentially and 14% year over year. Despite 200-400 MMcf/d of gas being shut in during the quarter because of weak Waha prices, volumes still increased by 450 MMcf/d from the first quarter. Most price-related curtailments returned in July, while producer activity remains strong. Targa Resources expects continued volume growth through the second half of 2026 and into 2027, supported by improving gas prices and better takeaway capacity. This growing throughput should support its gathering, processing and downstream businesses. Major Growth Projects Could Drive Significant Future EBITDA: Targa Resources has a substantial portfolio of organic projects that should expand its processing, transportation, fractionation and export capacity. Five Permian processing plants — Copperhead I and II, Yeti I and II, and Roadrunner III — are on track, while East Driver has already started operations ahead of schedule. Train 11 is online and highly utilized, with Trains 12 and 13 progressing. Speedway and the LPG export expansion are expected in the third quarter of 2027 and should provide meaningful operating leverage. Management expects these investments to support a strong EBITDA and free-cash-flow inflection over time. High Growth Capital Spending Could Pressure Free Cash Flow: Targa Resources' growth opportunity requires substantial capital investment, which could constrain free cash flow and shareholder returns in the near term. The company expects approximately $4.5 billion of net growth capital spending in 2026, compared with only $250 million of maintenance capital. Although these investments are designed to generate high returns and support future EBITDA growth, the scale of spending means the company remains heavily dependent on successful project execution and continued volume growth. Management itself expects the more meaningful free-cash-flow inflection to occur only after major projects such as Speedway and the LPG export expansion come online in the third quarter of 2027. Marketing Gains Are Likely to Moderate: A significant portion of TRGP's exceptional first-half performance came from market optimization opportunities that were not incorporated into its original guidance. Management indicated that the first half benefited from approximately $250 million of optimization margin, but expects materially lower marketing opportunities in the second half as basis spreads narrow and Waha gas prices improve. Management specifically acknowledged that the third quarter will face a headwind from weaker marketing benefits compared with the second quarter. Therefore, investors should not assume that the unusually strong marketing contribution seen earlier in 2026 will continue at the same level. Commodity Prices Still Create Some Earnings Exposure: Although Targa Resources has increasingly shifted its G&P contracts toward fee-based structures, part of its portfolio remains commodity-sensitive. Management noted that commodity prices were a slight headwind to G&P results during the second quarter, while the company also remains below aggregate fee-floor levels across its portfolio. A sustained improvement in gas and NGL prices could eventually provide a tailwind, but near-term earnings remain exposed to commodity-price movements and the balance between gas, NGL and crude economics. This creates some uncertainty around per-unit margins even when physical volumes continue to grow strongly. TRGP’s Premium Valuation: From a valuation perspective — in terms of Enterprise Value to Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA) ratio — Targa Resources is trading at a premium of 15.24 compared with the industry average of 12.35. The stock is also trading above its five-year mean of 12.02. Targa Resources remains a compelling midstream growth story, supported by its 20-year agreements with ExxonMobil, which provide strong long-term volume visibility along with strong stock performance as compared to peers like SUN and WES, while record Permian volumes and robust producer activity also support sustained growth. A substantial pipeline of processing, fractionation and export projects, along with positive 2026 earnings and revenue estimates, should strengthen EBITDA and free cash flow over time. However, these opportunities come with meaningful risks. TRGP’s approximately $4.5 billion of 2026 growth capital spending could constrain near-term free cash flow and make returns dependent on successful project execution. In addition, marketing gains are expected to moderate, while commodity-price exposure could create earnings volatility. The stock also trades at a premium valuation against its industry average. Given the company's attractive long-term growth prospects but limited margin for error at current valuation levels, retaining this Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) company appears prudent. Existing investors can benefit from future growth execution, while new investors may prefer to wait for a more attractive entry point or greater visibility on project returns and volume growth. title: Cenovus Energy is Undervalued: Should You Bet on the Stock Now? - theglobeandmail.com
content: Cenovus Energy Inc. CVE is currently considered undervalued on a relative basis, with the stock trading at 5.97x trailing 12-month Enterprise Value to Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EV/EBITDA), which is a discount compared with the broader industry average of 6.11x. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM and Chevron CVX, two other integrated energy majors, are valued at 9.24x and 7.76x, respectively. Such a discounted valuation often signals an entry point. However, before making investment decisions, one should consider the company's overall business environment and fundamentals. West Texas Intermediate (“WTI”) is currently trading above $85 per barrel, according to data from Oilprice.com, significantly higher than the shut-in and breakeven prices for existing wells in key resources. The escalation of conflicts in the Middle East has been aiding the rally in commodity prices. In its latest short-term energy outlook, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects the WTI spot price to average $80.88 per barrel this year, a level that should remain supportive of upstream operations.  As a result, CVE’s upstream operations are benefiting from higher benchmark oil prices, which are eventually increasing oil sands production. High oil prices are also benefiting other energy majors like XOM and CVX. Image Source: The U.S. Energy Information Administration On the second-quarter 2026 earnings call, management noted that CVE’s refining business remained strong, with Canadian and U.S. refinery utilization at about 94% and 96%, respectively, supported by strong operational availability and favorable refined-product pricing. Also, since it has exposure to Canadian heavy oil, which is cheaper than lighter crude, CVE is likely to be enjoying a feedstock cost advantage. In other words, the company’s Canadian refining business is capable of using lower-priced fuel to produce high-value end products, giving it an edge over other refiners and helping it continue its upward trajectory. Investors’ strong preference for the stock is getting reflected in the price chart. In the past year, CVE has jumped 117.1%, outperforming the industry’s 86.1% growth. XOM and CVX have surged 52.6% and 34.3%, respectively, over the same time frame. Investors should also know that Cenovus expects higher spending in the second half because of major refinery maintenance, while some large tax payments are due mainly in early 2027. It also relies heavily on outside condensate supplies and still faces uncertainty around Canada’s carbon-tax rules. Hence, investors shouldn’t rush to buy the stock. Those who have already invested may hold the stock. Cenovus Energy carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here. An integrated major carries barrels from the wellhead through refining and into chemicals, and ExxonMobil sits among the most recognizable examples of that structure. As the trading week reached its middle, the conversation around the stock leaned on how those layers fit together and how they might steady the company through the swings that define crude and natural gas. Guyana has become one of the most talked-about upstream regions in the world, and ExxonMobil operates at the heart of it. The offshore development in the Stabroek block has moved from exploration into a phase where new production vessels come online in sequence, each adding capacity to lift crude from deep water far off the coast. The appeal is straightforward in qualitative terms: the barrels tend to carry attractive per-unit economics, and the resource base has kept expanding as drilling confirms fresh discoveries. What makes the Guyana ramp-up notable this week is the cadence. Rather than a single burst of volume, the region is being brought forward in measured stages, with floating production units arriving one after another. That rhythm gives the company a runway of growing output without forcing a scramble, and it lets the operator refine its methods as each phase teaches something about the reservoir. For a company built around long-cycle projects, that steady progression is a familiar and comfortable pattern. If Guyana represents the offshore side of the growth narrative, the Permian Basin represents the onshore counterweight. Stretching across West Texas and southeastern New Mexico, the Permian remains the busiest oil-producing region in the country, and ExxonMobil has built a commanding position there. The addition of large adjacent acreage in recent times expanded the companys inventory of drilling locations and gave it more contiguous ground to work, which tends to lower the cost of moving equipment and laying gathering lines. Shale wells behave differently from deepwater projects. They come online quickly, decline quickly, and reward operators who can drill and complete at scale with tight cost control. ExxonMobil has leaned into that model, applying longer laterals and data-driven completion designs to squeeze more out of each section. The result is a Permian machine that can be dialed up or throttled back with more flexibility than the multi-year offshore developments, giving the company a useful lever as market conditions shift. The reason Guyana and the Permian keep coming up together is that both feed the same priority: durable cash generation. A business that spins off cash across the commodity cycle can fund its drilling program, sustain its dividend, and reduce debt without leaning too heavily on borrowing. That is the frame in which ExxonMobil is most often discussed, and it is why the pairing of low-cost offshore barrels with scalable onshore volumes draws so much notice. Cash generation also underwrites the companys habit of acquiring back stock over time. Dividends and buybacks together form the way large energy names distribute cash to the owners of their equity, and a company with two growing, low-cost supply sources is generally seen as better placed to keep that machinery running. None of this removes the sway of crude prices, but it does change the conversation from pure price-watching toward how efficiently the barrels are produced. An integrated major is more than an upstream driller. ExxonMobil refines crude into fuels, manufactures chemicals and specialty products, and markets those goods around the world. When crude prices climb, the upstream side tends to shine; when they fall, the downstream and chemicals arms can cushion the blow because their input costs ease. That natural hedge is the classic argument for the integrated structure, and it is a big part of why these companies are treated as core positions across the energy space. The chemicals arm, in particular, ties the company to broader industrial demand for plastics, packaging, and performance materials. It is a longer-cycle business that can smooth the sharper edges of commodity swings. Woven together, the upstream growth from Guyana and the Permian, the steadiness of refining, and the diversification of chemicals give ExxonMobil a spread of exposures that few pure-play drillers can match. The broader oil and gas backdrop is a study in cross-currents. Global demand for crude and refined fuels remains substantial, while the world simultaneously pushes toward cleaner sources of energy. That tension keeps the sector lively, and it shapes how capital is directed. Market watchers and operators alike track the balance between supply discipline among major producers and the pace of demand growth across transport, industry, and power generation. For anyone following oil and gas stocks, the way large majors navigate that balance is a recurring theme. ExxonMobils answer has leaned toward advantaged barrels, the low-cost, high-margin volumes that stay resilient even when prices soften. Guyana fits that description cleanly, and the best parts of the Permian do as well. The company has also placed bets on lower-carbon lines such as carbon capture and hydrogen, signaling that it intends to remain relevant as the energy mix evolves without abandoning the core that generates its cash today. Crude and natural gas prices have swung through wide ranges over recent seasons, driven by shifting supply decisions among major exporting nations, changing demand patterns, and the ripple effects of geopolitics. Natural gas has taken on added weight as liquefied exports connect once-regional markets into a more global web. For an integrated producer, this environment rewards flexibility and punishes overextension, and ExxonMobils mix of short-cycle shale and long-cycle offshore gives it options in both directions. The midweek tone around the stock reflects that reality. Rather than fixating on a single price print, the discussion has centered on how the company positions its volumes and how resilient its cash generation looks if prices wobble. That is a more durable way to frame an energy major, and it is consistent with how the largest names in the group are generally assessed. Within the peer set of global integrated majors, ExxonMobil is frequently described as one of the scale leaders, with a sprawling upstream portfolio, a heavy refining network, and a sizable chemicals arm. Its rivals pursue their own blends of offshore, onshore, and downstream exposure, and each has staked out a distinct path through the energy transition. As a component of the S&P 500, the company is a fixture in broad market-tracking portfolios, which keeps it in view even for those who do not follow energy closely. The competitive landscape is defined less by head-to-head rivalry over single assets and more by who can generate the most durable cash per barrel while keeping the balance sheet sturdy. On that measure, the combination of Guyanas economics and the Permians scale is exactly what keeps ExxonMobil near the front of the conversation among diversified producers. The developments drawing attention this week are cumulative rather than sudden. Each new production vessel offshore Guyana, each fresh batch of Permian wells, and each incremental step in cost efficiency adds to the narrative of growing, advantaged output. The company has also continued to talk up its longer-cycle projects and its lower-carbon ventures, framing itself as an operator that can grow supply today while preparing for a changing energy world. For observers, the takeaway is that the machine keeps advancing on multiple fronts at once. That breadth is part of why the stock stays in the midweek spotlight: there is rarely a moment when nothing is moving across such a large and varied portfolio. A recurring theme in how ExxonMobil is described is discipline. The company has spent recent seasons emphasizing structural cost reductions, tighter capital allocation, and a focus on the highest-margin barrels. In shale, that means drilling faster and completing smarter; offshore, it means standardizing designs so each new project builds on the last. The intent is to lower the break-even level at which the portfolio still generates healthy cash, which matters most when prices turn against producers. That operational focus is not glamorous, but it is central to the story. In a commodity business, the operators who survive downturns and thrive in upswings are usually the ones who kept their costs lean when times were good. ExxonMobils messaging has leaned hard into that idea, and it colors how the company is talked about even on quieter news days. That discipline shows up in the cadence of spending as well. By keeping its capital program steady and resisting the urge to chase every price spike, the company aims to smooth its path through the cycle so the drilling program and the distribution machinery can keep moving without sharp reversals. The advantaged nature of the Guyana and Permian barrels reinforces that steadiness, since low-cost volumes remain workable even when prices dip. It is a quiet kind of resilience, and it tends to matter most exactly when the sector turns turbulent and weaker operators are forced to retreat. The path is not without obstacles. The energy transition raises long-running questions about how demand for crude will evolve over the coming decades, and regulatory pressure around emissions continues to build in many regions. Price volatility remains a permanent feature of the business, and large projects always carry execution challenges, from weather offshore to supply-chain strains onshore. These are the headwinds every major must navigate, and ExxonMobil is no exception. The companys response has been to concentrate on advantaged resources and cost resilience while placing measured bets on lower-carbon technologies. That approach does not eliminate the challenges, but it aims to make the business more adaptable to whatever the period ahead brings. Booked barrels in Guyana keep expanding as the drill bit confirms fresh accumulations, while the dense acreage across the Permian carries a long inventory of locations that can be developed for many seasons. That combination of proven volumes and probable additions gives the company a runway that stretches well beyond any single trading period. Replacing produced barrels with new ones is the quiet arithmetic that keeps a producer alive across the decades, and the pairing of offshore discoveries with onshore inventory is exactly the kind of balance that keeps reserve life healthy. It is a slow-moving measure, rarely the subject of daily headlines, yet it underpins the confidence with which the company describes the many seasons of drilling that lie in front of it. The downstream half of the business rarely grabs headlines the way a new offshore vessel does, yet it carries real weight in how the company is understood. Refineries convert crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and feedstocks, and the margins earned on that processing move on a rhythm of their own, sometimes strengthening exactly when raw crude softens. The chemicals arm reaches further still, turning hydrocarbons into the plastics, packaging, and performance materials that flow into countless industrial supply chains. Because these operations consume the very commodity the upstream side offers, they form an internal counterweight that steadies the combined earnings base. Manufacturing and logistics networks spread across continents let the company move product toward wherever demand runs strongest, capturing value at several links of the chain rather than a single one. That breadth of processing and marketing is a defining trait of the integrated model, and it widens the base from which cash is generated. The march toward a lower-carbon energy mix sits over every large producer, and ExxonMobil has answered it by pairing its traditional barrels with measured steps into carbon capture, hydrogen, and lower-emission fuels. Rather than abandoning the core that generates its cash, the company frames these ventures as extensions of the engineering and project skills it already owns, aiming to lower the emissions intensity of its operations while staying relevant as the mix evolves. Regulatory pressure around flaring, methane, and reported emissions continues to build across many regions, and operators that treat those expectations as design constraints rather than afterthoughts tend to face fewer surprises. The energy transition is best read as a long arc rather than a sudden turn, and a company that can supply advantaged barrels today while preparing for a cleaner tomorrow is trying to keep a foot in both worlds. That balancing act frames much of how the name is discussed across the sector.  drew fresh attention midweek as energy names across the US market pushed toward record territory, standing out on a session when the broader tape turned softer. The move traced back to a tightening crude market, where escalating Middle East tension and a tense standoff around the Strait of Hormuz have reshaped how traders think about the flow of barrels. As one of the largest integrated energy companies in the world, ExxonMobil sits close to the center of that story, and its shares reflected the shift in sentiment as customers rotated toward producers with heavy exposure to oil and natural gas. The backdrop this week has been unusual. While much of the market drifted, the energy complex firmed, drawing strength from a crude benchmark that has climbed as shipping lanes came into question. The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow channel through which a large share of seaborne crude typically passes, has become the focal point of the current tension, and any hint of disruption there ripples quickly through global pricing. For a company with ExxonMobils scale, that dynamic tends to lift the value of every barrel it lifts. The company moves its production into a global market, so a firmer benchmark reaches across its entire producing base rather than a single region. Traders watching the tape midweek treated that reach as a reason to lean toward the largest producers, and ExxonMobil sits at the front of that queue by sheer size. Crude does not trade in isolation from geopolitics, and the current episode makes that point plainly. Reports of tankers rerouting, of proposed bypass corridors, and of vessels avoiding the chokepoint have kept a firm bid under the benchmark. When the market perceives that supply could tighten, the price of oil tends to rise even before any physical shortfall appears, because customers move early to secure barrels. That anticipatory behavior has been on display this week, and it has fed directly into the tone across energy equities. For ExxonMobil, the mechanism is straightforward. The company produces crude and natural gas around the world, and higher benchmark pricing lifts the realized value of that output. At the same time, a tighter market tends to widen the spreads that refiners capture when they turn crude into fuels, a dynamic that touches the downstream side of the business. The combination is why an integrated major often behaves as a barometer for the entire complex when tension flares. Because ExxonMobil touches nearly every stage of the value chain, its shares tend to absorb signals from both crude and fuels at once, giving the market a single, closely watched reference point for how the whole sector is faring. That role as a bellwether has been on clear display through the current stretch of firm pricing. ExxonMobil operates across the full energy chain. Its upstream arm explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas across a wide geographic footprint, spanning onshore basins, deepwater developments, and liquefied natural gas ventures. Its downstream arm refines crude into gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and other products, while its chemical business converts hydrocarbons into the building blocks used across manufacturing. That breadth is central to how the company weathers swings in any single link of the chain. The integrated structure gives the company a degree of balance. When crude prices climb, the upstream side captures the upside. When margins on fuels widen, the refining side benefits. And when petrochemical demand firms, the chemical segment adds another stream. This week, with crude firm and the sector strong, the parts of the business tied most directly to oil pricing have been the ones drawing the spotlight. Reinforcing the tone around the stock, ExxonMobil reported very strong results in its most recent quarter. The company generated robust cash from its operations, supported by firm commodity pricing and steady volumes across its core producing regions. Management has spent recent years reshaping the portfolio toward lower-cost, higher-yielding barrels, and the most recent period showed that work translating into strong headline figures. The refining side of the business contributed as well, with the company processing crude into fuels at a time when demand for transportation products stayed firm. Chemical operations added their own contribution, rounding out a quarter in which each major segment played a part. The strength of the report gave the market a fundamental anchor to pair with the geopolitical story, and the two together framed much of the midweek move. The downstream business deserves a closer look because it often gets overshadowed by the drama of crude prices. Refining margins depend on the gap between the cost of crude feedstock and the price of finished fuels, and that gap can widen sharply when supply concerns collide with steady demand. ExxonMobil operates a large, globally distributed refining network, and that scale lets it capture value across many markets at once. During periods of tension like the current one, the downstream arm can act as a stabilizer. Even as crude costs rise, strong demand for gasoline and diesel can keep the finished-product side healthy. That balance is part of why integrated majors tend to stay resilient when the energy complex firms, and it helps explain the resilience ExxonMobil has shown this week relative to the softer broad market. On the upstream side, ExxonMobil has concentrated its efforts on a handful of high-quality regions. Its position in the Permian basin of the US anchors its onshore output, delivering barrels at a cost structure the company has worked hard to lower. Offshore, its developments in Guyana have become a signature growth engine, ramping crude output from a series of deepwater projects that rank among the most closely watched in the industry. Liquefied natural gas ventures add a further dimension, connecting the company to markets far from its producing basins. Together, these engines give ExxonMobil a base of output that it can grow while keeping spending disciplined. In a week when crude pricing is firm, the value of that output rises, and the market has taken notice. Each of these regions carries a distinct cost profile, and the blend of onshore shale, deepwater crude, and liquefied gas gives the company a spread of exposures that few peers can match. That diversity of supply sources helps smooth the swings that come with any one basin, and it lets the company keep growing output while spending stays measured. The wider market has been mixed this week, with the S&P 500 drifting as attention rotated across sectors. Against that softer backdrop, energy stood out, and ExxonMobils move reflected the divergence. When the broad tape cools while one sector firms, it often signals that a specific theme is capturing capital, and the current crude tightening is exactly that kind of theme. Rotation of this sort is a familiar feature of energy markets. When geopolitics push crude higher, capital tends to flow toward the companies most levered to oil pricing, and the majors sit near the top of that list. ExxonMobil, as one of the most prominent names in the group, naturally draws attention when the rotation gathers pace. The broad basket of energy stocks has firmed as crude tightened, and the groups move toward record territory has been one of the defining features of the week. Within that basket, the integrated majors carry outsized weight because of their scale, and ExxonMobil ranks among the heaviest. When the sector runs, a company of its size tends to run with it, and the current stretch has been no exception. Sector strength of this kind reflects more than a single headline. It draws on the sense that firm crude pricing supports the entire chain, from wellhead to refinery gate. That breadth is why energy has been able to press higher even as other corners of the market lost momentum midweek. The sectors move toward records has been broad rather than narrow, reaching producers, refiners, and the service names that support them. When a rally stretches across so many corners of a single group at once, it tends to reflect a shared read on the direction of crude, and that shared read has kept the group firm through the week. Within the group of integrated majors, ExxonMobil occupies a distinctive place. Its combination of scale, geographic reach, and integration across the value chain gives it a broad base from which to operate. The company has spent recent years trimming costs, concentrating capital on its strongest assets, and streamlining its structure, and that work has sharpened how it competes against its peers. That positioning matters most when the market turns its focus to fundamentals. A company with low-cost barrels and a disciplined spending approach tends to generate strong cash across a range of price environments. When crude firms on top of that base, the effect compounds, and the strength shows up in results like those reported in the most recent quarter. Beyond the immediate crude story, several threads have shaped the picture around ExxonMobil. The continued ramp of its Guyana developments remains a central storyline, as each new phase adds barrels at attractive cost. Its Permian program continues to deliver steady onshore output, and its liquefied natural gas ventures keep expanding the companys reach into global gas markets. Each of these threads feeds the same narrative of disciplined growth. The company has also pressed forward with efforts to lower emissions intensity and to build out lower-carbon business lines, areas that have grown in importance across the industry. While crude pricing dominates the headlines this week, these longer-running initiatives form part of how the company frames its direction, and they add context to the broader story around the stock. A recurring theme in ExxonMobils approach has been discipline. Rather than chasing volume at any cost, the company has emphasized capital efficiency, directing spending toward the projects that deliver the strongest economics. That discipline shows up in a cost structure that has come down over recent years, allowing the company to generate strong cash even when crude is not at extreme levels. When crude firms, as it has this week, that discipline amplifies the effect. Lower costs mean more of each incremental dollar of revenue flows through to cash generation. The most recent quarter offered a clear illustration, with strong results built on a foundation of disciplined operations rather than on price alone. The industry is not without its complications. Crude pricing is inherently volatile, and the same geopolitical tension lifting prices this week could reverse if the standoff eases. Regulatory pressures, shifting demand patterns, and the long transition toward lower-carbon energy all shape how the majors plan. ExxonMobil, like its peers, must navigate these currents while keeping its core business healthy. Supply-chain constraints, cost inflation in certain services, and the challenge of replacing produced reserves add further complexity. These are the persistent features of the energy business, and they temper any simple reading of a strong week. Still, the companys scale and discipline give it a broad base from which to manage these challenges. The strength in ExxonMobil and its peers carries meaning beyond the sector itself. Energy prices feed into inflation, into consumer spending, and into the calculations that shape the broad market. When crude firms sharply, the effects ripple outward, touching everything from transportation costs to the tone of the wider tape. That is part of why a crude-driven rally in energy names draws attention well beyond the group. For the market as a whole, the current episode is a reminder of how quickly geopolitics can reshape sentiment. A standoff around a single waterway has firmed crude, lifted the energy complex, and pushed a name like ExxonMobil into the spotlight. As the week unfolds, the interplay between the geopolitical story and the fundamental strength shown in the most recent quarter will continue to frame how the market reads the stock. title: Exxon Stock Surges 2.3% as Oil Breaks Above $91 - TradingView
content: Exxon Mobil XOM, one of the world's largest integrated energy companies, jumped approximately 2.3% in Tuesday morning as oil prices pushed higher on renewed geopolitical fears. Reuters reported that crude extended its advance after Washington rejected an extension of the expired U.S.-Iran ceasefire, reviving concerns about potential supply disruptions. Exxon is entering this oil rally with a business already firing on all cylinders. The company reported second-quarter earnings of $14.5 billion, adjusted earnings of $14.7 billion, and free cash flow of $17.2 billion. Production reached its strongest level in more than two decades outside major Middle East disruptions, while Permian Basin output continued hitting new records. The bigger story is that Exxon is no longer just a bet on higher oil prices it is a cash machine built to benefit when energy markets tighten. Every additional dollar in crude prices flows directly into the company's upstream economics, while strong refining margins provide another layer of support. However, the GF Value chart highlights the key investor question. Exxon shares traded at $164.65 compared with a GF Value estimate of $125.23, showing the stock was trading 31.47% above its estimated intrinsic value. The market is rewarding Exxon's production strength, balance sheet, and commodity exposure, but investors are also paying for today's geopolitical premium. Exxon has built one of the strongest operating platforms in global energy. The company's fundamentals are doing the heavy lifting but the next move in the stock may depend on whether oil stays elevated or whether geopolitical tensions cool faster than expected. title: XOM Runs One Of The Market’s Biggest Cash-Return Machines - Trefis
content: A quiet energy giant has been running one of the market’s great cash machines, but what did that torrent of money actually buy for its owners? ExxonMobil (XOM) stock trades around $161.46 a share, having delivered a +56% return over the last twelve months. But beneath the share price is a capital-return engine of almost unrivaled scale. Over the last five years, the company has handed back $163 billion in cash to its shareholders. The sheer size of that payout, one of the largest in the market, forces a sharp question for any owner: the company returned a fortune, but was holding the stock worth it, and is it now? The $163 billion figure, equal to about 24% of the company’s current market value, is huge. It is the 5th largest cash return of any U.S. company over the period, dwarfing the $5.8 billion returned by the median S&P 500 firm. The sum was split between $80 billion in dividends and $83 billion in share repurchases. This isn’t financial engineering. The cash is the direct result of a sprawling, integrated operation firing on all cylinders. Management pointed to strong performance across the company in its latest update, from record second-quarter diesel production in its Energy Products business to its highest non-Middle East upstream production volumes in over two decades. In the Permian basin, production hit a record of more than 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels per day, driven by deploying new technology at scale. For shareholders, the results of this capital discipline have been clear. Over the same five-year period, ExxonMobil stock delivered a total return of +241%, dramatically outperforming the S&P 500’s +87% return. But the honest catch is that every dollar returned to owners is a dollar not reinvested into the business for future growth. This is a deliberate choice, reflected in the company’s 3-year average annual revenue growth of 0.0%. Is this a sign of a business out of new ideas, or a disciplined focus on only the most profitable projects? Management consistently emphasizes a focus on “value, not volume.” This strategic priority is a recurring theme, as explored in a recent analysis titled Reading Between The Lines Of XOM’s Latest Call. For investors who prefer exposure to the entire sector rather than a single company’s strategy, an oil and gas ETF offers a broader approach. The test for owners is the cash inflection in Guyana. The sustainability of these returns depends on the company’s most advantaged growth projects, and none is more critical than its development in Guyana. Management calls it a “real success story,” noting that the company is “recovering our capital and cost nearly two years earlier than anticipated.” Beyond being good news, this development is a turning point for cash generation. As the initial investment is paid down, the project is set for what management describes as an “inflection in free cash flow.” The specific thing for owners to watch is the progress of the production vessels that unlock this cash. The fifth vessel is on track for start-up by the end of the year. Its successful deployment is the most tangible proof that this cash-return machine is built to last. With a payout ratio of around 70%, it also has plenty of room to continue raising its dividend, as it has in the past. Verizon has boosted its payout for an impressive 20 consecutive years. RSI at 63.8 is still technically neutral, not yet in the classic overbought zone, but it is leaning toward the stronger end of the range. More importantly, Stochastic %K at 87.5 and %D at 82.6 are both in overbought territory, as shown in the chart. That usually does not mean an immediate reversal; it means the stock has risen quickly enough that short-term traders may start taking profits unless fresh demand keeps arriving. XOM is trading near the top band at 161.77, with %B at 98%, which means price is hugging the upper edge of the band rather than sitting in the middle. That often happens during strong advances, but it also means the stock is near an area where a pause is statistically more likely. The 7.9% band width is narrowing, pointing to a squeeze, which often precedes a larger move. In practical terms, the stock is coiling: if buyers keep pushing, the next move can be sharp; if they stall, the stock can snap back toward the middle band at 155.60. Volume does not yet fully confirm the breakout tone. The latest volume of 10,231,300 is only 0.7× the 20-hour average of 13,952,955, and OBV is falling. OBV, or on-balance volume, tracks whether volume is flowing with price; when it drops while price rises, it can mean the advance is being driven more by price momentum than by broad participation. That does not break the trend, but it does argue for caution near resistance. The chart leaves a fairly clear map. Immediate support sits at 148.36, while the more relevant near-term pivot is the SMA20 at 155.60, which also matches the Bollinger middle band. If XOM holds above that area, the trend remains intact and the recent move looks like a continuation rather than a spike. If it loses that zone, the stock would likely be testing whether the rally was overextended. On the upside, the first meaningful barrier is the 160.10 resistance, followed by the 163.68 three-month high. A clean hold above resistance would strengthen the case that the squeeze is resolving upward. Failure to sustain above that line would instead suggest the stock is still trading inside a capped range, even if the longer trend remains positive. HOLD (wait & see) — the trend is positive, but the stock is also stretched near the upper Bollinger band and overbought on Stochastic, while volume and OBV are not yet confirming the latest push. - MACD remains positive, so the trend still has momentum behind it.
- Price is above the SMA20 and SMA50, which keeps the broader structure constructive.

title: US-Israel Strikes On Iran Send Nasdaq, S&P 500 Futures Lower As Offensive Continues Across The Middle East — LMT, RTX, XOM, USO, BATL On Traders' Radar Today - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock futures were lower early Monday amid the escalation of tensions in the Middle East following attacks by the United States and Israel on Iran. The strikes on Iran killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on Saturday. Subsequent updates from the Israeli administration’s official channels, including its military and air force, highlighted the killings of several others in Iran’s political and intelligence apparatus. Iran’s ambassador to the International Atomic Energy Agency stated that the country’s nuclear site at Natanz has been hit in the U.S.-Israel strikes, according to a Reuters report. As of 5:30 a.m. ET on Monday, S&P futures traded 1% lower, Dow futures were down 1.1%, and Nasdaq futures declined 1.4%, while Russell 2000 futures lost 1.2%. Meanwhile, retail sentiment toward the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) has remained ‘bullish’, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ETF, which tracks the Nasdaq 100 Index, has remained ‘neutral’. Crude oil prices rose to an eight-month high on Monday following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. At the time of writing, U.S. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures maturing in April were up 7.5% to $72 per barrel. Brent crude futures maturing in May gained 8% to $78.7 per barrel. Analysts at ING Think pointed out that while the U.S. has limited trade exposure to the Strait of Hormuz, its closure would fuel an increase in global oil prices, exacerbating the current cost-of-living crisis. “U.S. consumers are already stretched, and gasoline prices are acutely politically sensitive going into midterm territory. Higher oil prices would also complicate the Federal Reserve's future monetary policy path,” the firm stated in its latest note. Lockheed Martin (LMT), RTX (RTX), Northrop Grumman (NOC): Defense stocks soared in Monday’s pre-market trade, gaining between 6% and 8% amid the rising tensions in the Middle East. Exxon Mobil (XOM), Battalion Oil (BATL), Chevron (CVX): Exxon Mobil and Chevron stocks rose about 5% in Monday’s pre-market session amid a boil in oil prices during the Iran conflict. Battalion Oil shares soared about 85%, continuing to trend upward and building on the 33% gains the stock registered on Friday. Crude oil ETFs also saw an uptick. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK-A, BRK-B): Berkshire Hathaway’s shares were down about 2% pre-market on Monday after the company’s fourth-quarter (Q4) results missed Wall Street expectations. Berkshire reported earnings per share (EPS) of $4.73 on Saturday, missing an expected EPS of $5.51, according to Fiscal.ai data. Berkshire CEO Greg Abel stated that the company is “evaluating opportunities” regarding its cash position. HOOD’s stock was down over 3.3% in pre-market trade on Monday, on track to kick off March in the red, amid broader weakness in markets after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran over the weekend and U.S. President Donald Trump stated that the “combat operation” would not stop until “all objectives” were met. During its fourth quarter (Q4) results in February, Robinhood reported that crypto-related transaction revenue dropped 38% year-over-year to $221 million. The company said the drop was driven by lower trading activity and lower crypto prices, which in turn caused the firm to miss revenue forecasts. Overall, Robinhood reported earnings of $0.66 per share, missing analyst expectations of $0.68, as per Koyfin data. Revenue came in at $1.28 billion, also missing the consensus estimate of $1.34 billion. In comparison to HOOD’s price drop of nearly 33%, Bitcoin’s price has only fallen around 25% so far this year. Hang Seng Sinks As US–Iran Conflict Rattles Chinese Tech Comments posted here will also appear on symbol pages. Shares of CoreWeave, Inc. (CRWV) fell 4% in premarket trading on Monday after “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry warned the company resembles past tech bubble plays, even as analysts remained bullish on long-term growth. CRWV stock fell over 18% on Friday to $79.56, marking its worst session in over six months, and fell another 0.2% in extended trade. In a Substack note on Friday, Burry said CoreWeave “exists as an off-balance sheet SPV [special purpose vehicle] designed to lose money,” adding that enthusiasm around AI spending had pushed the company into public markets. He compared the business model to Level 3 Communications during the last technology bubble, saying that CoreWeave may be in an even more challenging position because its infrastructure depreciates faster. Burry added that the company’s infrastructure economics could prove more demanding over time, suggesting the comparison was “so obvious it is almost not interesting enough to discuss.” The remarks came shortly after CoreWeave reported fourth-quarter (Q4) results that missed expectations and outlined plans for higher investment. The company posted a Q4 loss of $0.56 per share on revenue of $1.57 billion, compared with expectations for a $0.49 loss on $1.53 billion in revenue, according to Fiscal.ai data. At the same time, CoreWeave projected capital expenditures of $30 billion to $35 billion for 2026, more than double the $14.9 billion spent in 2025. Its first-quarter revenue outlook of $1.9 billion to $2 billion also fell short of Wall Street’s $2.24 billion estimate. CEO Mike Intrator defended the company’s spending plans, telling CNBC that demand for infrastructure has been “relentless” as enterprise and sovereign customers scale AI deployments. “Our clients are increasing the demand signals that they are giving us,” Intrator said, adding that the company had made an “intentional decision” to expand infrastructure even if it pressures margins. He also acknowledged investor concerns around the scale of the company’s spending, but said the investment reflects an “enormous” backlog. Following the earnings miss and capital intensity outlook, JPMorgan lowered its target to $90 from $110, implying an upside of about 18.5% from the stock’s last close, while maintaining a Neutral rating. The brokerage cited a more “pronounced” investment cycle. Mizuho cut its target to $95 from $100, suggesting an upside of roughly 25.1% from current levels. The S&P 500 has edged just 0.49% higher so far this year while the Nasdaq has fallen 2.47%. Silver, in comparison, has gained more than 33% while gold’s price have surged more than 20%. “I do not like the price action in U.S. – and especially U.S. Tech – equities, which struggle to reach new highs. Were these to correct significantly, I think this would bring BTC below $60k,” Barthere warned. Bitcoin’s price tumbled 2.2% in the last 24hours, falling below $66,000. (TSLA) shares fell about 4% in overnight trading heading into Monday after the company raised the price of its newly introduced entry-level Cybertruck, reversing a brief period when the electric pickup was offered at its lowest-ever starting price. Tesla launched its most affordable Cybertruck on Feb. 20 with a starting price of $59,990, positioning it below previous trims and closer to long-standing expectations of broader accessibility. However, effective March 1, the company increased the starting price to $69,990, marking a 17% jump and eliminating the temporary discount window that had lasted just 10 days. CEO Elon Musk had indicated at launch on X that the promotional pricing would be available only briefly, noting that the eventual price would depend on demand. The adjustment also returns the entry-level configuration to the same pricing level as the rear-wheel-drive version Tesla discontinued in September 2025. The company has also removed the lease option for the newly launched variant. With the latest revision, Tesla’s Cybertruck range resets across three tiers. The entry dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) version now begins at $69,990, while the premium AWD trim remains priced at $79,990 and the tri-motor Cyberbeast sits at $99,990. When the Cybertruck was unveiled in 2019, Musk projected a starting price of about $39,990, with the most advanced configuration expected to begin near $70,000. When production finally began in November 2023, actual pricing entered the market well above those early projections. The lower-priced variant retains the same dual-motor powertrain and roughly 325-mile estimated range as the premium AWD model, but its original cost savings were achieved through a simplified interior and reduced feature set. Compared with higher trims, it substitutes textile seating for premium materials, pares back audio and comfort features, and replaces air suspension with coil springs, while also removing certain cabin technology elements. Cybertruck sales have so far fallen short of Tesla’s early ambitions. Around 20,000 units were sold in the U.S. last year, far below initial production targets. The company does not disclose Cybertruck deliveries separately; instead, it groups them within its “other models” category alongside the Model S and Model X. Despite this, updated ordering timelines now suggest delivery wait times stretching into 2027 for the entry AWD version in some U.S. regions. Alongside pricing adjustments, Tesla highlighted progress in its Full Self-Driving Supervised (FSD) system, which has now logged more than 8.4 billion cumulative miles, according to company data. Musk has previously said that roughly 10 billion miles of real-world driving data may be needed to support safe unsupervised autonomy at scale. During Tesla’s fourth-quarter earnings call, Musk also said the Cybertruck platform could be used for autonomous intra-city cargo delivery, calling it suitable for short-distance urban logistics if consumer demand for the vehicle falls short of expectations.
